analysis.one_liner: Taxes coal, oil, and natural gas based on their carbon content to cut carbon dioxide emissions.
analysis.headline: A carbon tax on coal, oil, and natural gas never left the House tax committee, dying there with zero cosponsors when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a new tax to the tax code on coal, petroleum, and natural gas, charged at the producer or importer level and scaled to each fuel's carbon content — the highest rate on coal, the most carbon-intensive fuel. Rates would have started low in 1994 and phased up over four years, then risen with inflation. Its stated purpose was to reduce carbon dioxide emissions.
analysis.who_benefits: The public would gain reduced carbon dioxide emissions, with the largest emitters — coal first — paying the highest rates. Revenue would flow to the Treasury from the fuels driving climate change, and the rates would rise automatically with inflation so the incentive to cut emissions would not erode over time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, via lower carbon emissions

how_it_helps.text: The bill's stated purpose is to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by putting a price on the carbon content of coal, petroleum, and natural gas — the three fossil fuels behind most U.S. energy emissions.

The rates phase in over four years rather than hitting all at once: the coal tax starts at $3.60 per ton in 1994 and rises to $18 per ton; petroleum starts at 78 cents per barrel and rises to $3.90; natural gas starts at 9.6 cents per MCF and rises to 48 cents.
The tax rates are indexed to inflation after 1994, so the emission-reduction incentive would not fade in real-dollar terms over time.
The tax is collected from producers, importers, and pipeline operators rather than from individual consumers at the point of sale, keeping administration simple.

analysis.who_pays: Producers and importers of coal, petroleum, and natural gas would owe the new tax directly. In practice, an excise tax on fuel is passed along in prices, so households would also pay more for gasoline, electricity, and home heating.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal, oil, gas producers; then consumers

drawbacks.text: The bill offers no rebates or offsetting tax cuts, so the fuel tax would reach households through higher prices for gasoline, electricity, and home heating — costs that take a larger share of a low-income family's budget.

Because coal is taxed at the highest rate, the burden falls most heavily on coal-producing regions and coal-dependent utilities, affecting the jobs and electricity bills of the communities that rely on them.
The bill drew no cosponsors from either party, suggesting even allies saw no path for it; a carbon tax introduced alone, with no broader package to return the revenue, faced long odds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a simple, direct carbon tax: it prices the fuels by how much carbon dioxide they produce, phases in gradually, and indexes to inflation. Its main weakness is distribution — with no rebate or offsetting cut, the higher fuel and electricity prices would fall on all households, hitting lower-income families hardest, while the emission benefits are shared broadly and arrive over time. Whether that trade is worth making was never tested, because the bill never even reached a committee hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the tax-writing committee the day it was introduced and never came out; it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the carbon tax bill on February 3, 1993 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, which is where tax bills must begin.
No member of the House cosponsored the bill at any point during the two-year Congress.
The Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill, and it received no hearing, no floor vote, and no Senate counterpart action before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers came out ahead: no carbon tax ever took effect, so coal, oil, and natural gas continued to be sold untaxed by carbon content. Consumers also came out ahead in the short run, avoiding the higher gasoline, electricity, and heating prices the tax would have passed through.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers; short-run energy consumers

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the carbon tax bill on February 3, 1993 and spoke for it on the House floor

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral the day it was introduced and took no further action on it before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the bill's only support in the record was its single Democratic sponsor — no member of either party cosponsored it.

industries.note: Coal faced the highest rate of the three fuels — $18 per ton once fully phased in — because it releases the most carbon dioxide per unit of energy. The tax would have raised coal's cost and squeezed the industry hardest.

A new $3.90-per-barrel tax on petroleum and petroleum products, including crude oil, would have been owed at the same taxable events as the existing petroleum tax, raising costs throughout the oil supply chain.
A 48-cent-per-thousand-cubic-feet tax on natural gas delivered at pipeline facilities or imported, including natural gas liquids, would have raised costs for gas producers and pipeline operators.
Utilities burning coal or gas for power would have paid the fuel taxes and passed them to electricity customers, giving a relative advantage to lower-carbon generation sources.
